subject: Medicine
summary: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine‑secreting tumour of adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. It causes episodic hypertension and the classic 5 Ps, and can be life‑threatening if untreated.

sections.p: A tumour of adrenal medulla chromaffin cells that releases excess norepinephrine, epinephrine and dopamine. Diagnosis rests on biochemical proof of catecholamine excess plus imaging.

t.b: Does the patient have sustained catecholamine excess? Elevated levels confirm biochemical diagnosis.
Is there a rapid, sensitive screen for excess catecholamines? High levels strongly suggest PCC; normal result makes disease unlikely.
Where is the tumour located? Shows adrenal mass; MRI better for extra‑adrenal lesions.
Is the lesion functionally active or extra‑adrenal? Detects catecholamine‑avid tissue when CT/MRI equivocal.
Is there an inherited syndrome? Guides family screening and surgical planning.

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM system for adrenal tumours; malignancy is defined by metastasis, not size alone. The ‘Rule of 10%’ helps estimate risk of bilateral, extra‑adrenal, familial or malignant disease.
Most are sporadic, but hereditary syndromes are common enough to test for.
Classic episodic triad of headache, sweating and palpitations, often with paroxysmal hypertension. The 5 Ps help recall the full picture.
Biochemistry first, then localisation. In low‑resource settings, plasma metanephrines may be unavailable; a 24‑h urine collection is the fallback.
b: If catecholamine tests unavailable, treat presumptively with alpha‑blockade before surgery.

t.b: Can we still confirm excess catecholamines? Elevated levels support diagnosis.
Is the patient hyperglycaemic from catecholamine effect? Guides peri‑operative glucose management.

sections.p: Uncontrolled catecholamine surges can precipitate hypertensive crises, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, stroke, or pulmonary oedema.
b: Sudden severe headache with visual changes → possible intracranial bleed
Chest pain with tachyarrhythmia → risk of MI
Pulmonary oedema from acute left‑ventricular failure

sections.p: Control catecholamine effects before tumour removal. Alpha‑blockade first, then beta‑blockade, then definitive surgery.
b: Non‑selective irreversible α‑blocker (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) to prevent vasoconstriction
Selective β‑blocker only after adequate α‑blockade to control tachycardia
Laparoscopic adrenalectomy for most adrenal lesions; open surgery for large or invasive tumours
Avoid β‑blockade alone – can cause unopposed α‑stimulation and crisis

sections.p: Lifelong surveillance because recurrence or new tumours can appear, especially in hereditary cases.
b: Annual plasma metanephrines or 24‑h urine for 10 years, then every 2–3 years
Genetic counselling for patients with MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx
Blood pressure monitoring; treat residual hypertension

sections.p: Other causes of paroxysmal hypertension or the 5 Ps.
Certain conditions can cause false‑positive or false‑negative catecholamine tests.
b: Stress, severe pain, or certain drugs (tricyclic antidepressants, labetalol) raise catecholamines → false positive
Improper urine collection (incomplete 24 h) → false negative
Renal failure reduces clearance of metanephrines → may exaggerate levels

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache with visual loss
Sudden rise in blood pressure >180/120 mmHg

faq.a: Alpha blockade prevents vasoconstriction; giving beta‑blockade first leaves unopposed alpha activity, risking hypertensive crisis.

faq.q: Can a normal plasma metanephrine rule out PCC?
faq.a: A normal result makes PCC unlikely, but rare false negatives occur if the tumour is small or intermittent.

faq.q: Is surgery curative for malignant PCC?
faq.a: Surgery removes the primary tumour, but metastatic disease may need additional therapies (e.g., MIBG therapy, chemotherapy).

exam: Explain the diagnostic algorithm for a patient with episodic hypertension and the 5 Ps.
Describe the pharmacologic preparation for pheochromocytoma surgery and why the order of drugs matters.
List the hereditary syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma and the implications for family screening.
